proposal: Single-register quantum Fourier sampling is already ruled out for permutation equivalence of binary self-dual codes (length n, dimension k = n/2) by the theorem of Dinh, Moore and Russell, which shows that code-equivalence coset states over (GL_k(F_q) × S_n) ≀ Z_2 carry negligible information about the hidden permutation. Researchers can therefore cite that theorem and drop Fourier sampling for self-dual instances.
killer: The Dinh–Moore–Russell result is a sufficient condition whose hypotheses include q^(k^2) ≤ n^(0.2n), together with small automorphism groups and large minimal degree. For q = 2 and k = n/2 the left side is 2^(n^2/4), far above n^(0.2n) = 2^(0.2 n log n), so the theorem says nothing about self-dual codes and a different argument is needed.
lesson: Check every hypothesis of a no-go theorem (dimension bounds, automorphism size, minimal degree) against the actual parameters; a violated hypothesis leaves the case open rather than settled either way.
note: Kept one copy; the self-dual-k24 and self-dual-k32 records are identical and were rejected as duplicates.

proposal: In a classical audit of an S_n-symmetric multi-copy measurement, each typical isotypic block is a matrix with dim(V_λ) rows and b·dim(W_μ) columns, where V_λ and W_μ are irreducible representations and b is the number of hypotheses. Tracing over the multiplicity space W_μ leaves one live column per hypothesis, shrinking each block to b columns, so the audit becomes polynomial-time for typical shapes λ and μ.
killer: Only the column count shrinks: every block keeps all dim(V_λ) of its rows; for Plancherel-typical partitions dim(V_λ) is about sqrt(n!)·e^(-O(sqrt n)), superexponential in n. Without a separate symbolic or tensor-network compression of V_λ itself the audit stays exponential.
lesson: Count every tensor factor of a representation-theoretic block: removing a multiplicity factor does not help when the irreducible dimension itself is exponential for typical shapes.

proposal: Some trimmed sub-POVM on polynomially many coset states is known to identify the hidden permutation in self-dual code equivalence, viewed as a hidden subgroup problem in a wreath product of symmetric groups. Implement it generically: block-encode the needed operator by a PREPARE/SELECT linear combination of the group-action unitaries and apply a polynomial-degree low-pass QSVT filter onto the informative spectral window, for a polynomial-cost measurement.
killer: A filter that touches the group action only as a black box can be used to locate one marked permutation among n! candidates, so the BBBV unstructured-search lower bound forces Ω(sqrt(n!)) queries. Knowing that a good POVM exists says nothing about implementing it; an efficient filter must exploit specific representation structure of these coset states.
lesson: A generic LCU or QSVT filter inherits unstructured-search lower bounds unless it uses representation-specific structure; existence of a measurement is not an implementation.

proposal: Regev's reduction from the dihedral coset problem to average-case subset sum calls the subset-sum solver coherently to disentangle a superposition over two solution strings of the same instance (the matching step). Conjecture: this step needs a deterministic solver, since a solver for the relation that returns any one of several solutions using internal randomness would leave different garbage on the two branches and destroy their relative phase.
killer: Purify the randomized solver and evaluate it on both endpoints in a fixed order, then measure only the unordered pair of witnesses; each orientation picks up the same product of solver amplitudes and the leftover garbage depends only on the ordered pair, so the interference survives. Randomized relation solvers therefore compose with the matching step at the cost of a second solver call.
lesson: Branch-dependent garbage from a randomized subroutine can often be removed by purifying it and evaluating it symmetrically on every superposed input before measuring a symmetric label.

proposal: After m phase states of the dihedral hidden subgroup problem are combined, the pretty good measurement amounts to reweighting each subset-sum fiber (the bit strings sharing one weighted sum) by the inverse square root of its size. Block-encode the fiber sizes, or the matching amplitudes, of the standard encoding as singular values and apply a polynomial-degree QSVT approximation of x ↦ x^(-1/2) to realize the measurement in polynomial time.
killer: The block encoding is normalized by 2^m, so fibers of size one and two appear as singular values only about 2^-m apart (2^-(m/2) in the amplitude encoding) while their required weights differ by a constant. Markov's inequality says a bounded polynomial whose value moves by a constant across a gap δ has degree Ω(1/sqrt δ), giving degree Ω(2^(m/2)) or Ω(2^(m/4)), exponential in m.
lesson: QSVT cannot cheaply separate singular values that a block-encoding normalization squeezes exponentially close together; look for encodings whose normalization keeps the relevant gaps inverse-polynomial.

proposal: In the dihedral coset problem, the interference step groups bit strings b ∈ {0,1}^m by the weighted sum Σ b_i k_i mod N with N ≈ 2^m. Write this grouping as a matrix-product operator that sweeps over the m bits and carries the exact running residue on its bond; since only residues that actually occur need storing, the bond dimension should stay polynomial, so the grouping-and-interference map can be built and contracted classically in polynomial time.
killer: The bond after i sites must distinguish every distinct prefix sum Σ_{j≤i} b_j k_j mod N, and for random k_j the 2^i prefix sums are pairwise distinct with high probability for i up to a constant fraction of m, by the birthday bound since N is about 2^m. The bond dimension is therefore 2^Ω(m): the exact network is the pseudo-polynomial subset-sum dynamic program over N residues.
lesson: An exact tensor network that tracks a modular sum inherits the size of the residue space; polynomial bond dimension needs hashing or approximation with a proven error.

proposal: In a K-copy coset-state measurement for a symmetric-group hidden subgroup problem, weak Fourier sampling first gives each copy an irreducible-representation label of S_n, and the remaining measurement is invariant under permuting the K copies. Decomposing under this copy-permutation symmetry (Schur–Weyl duality over the copies) should leave only polynomial-size matrices, giving an efficient final measurement at polynomial K while keeping every irrep label.
killer: Copy-permutation symmetry compresses only when copies share types: with r distinct label categories the symmetric sector grows like binomial(K+cr−1, cr−1), polynomial in K only for fixed r. With full irrep labels each Plancherel probability is at most max d_λ^2/n!, superpolynomially small, so polynomially many copies carry pairwise distinct labels with high probability, the stabilizer in S_K is trivial, and a 2^K-size block remains.
lesson: Symmetry under permuting copies yields polynomial compression only for a bounded number of distinct copy types; check how often labels collide before relying on it.

proposal: The no-go theorem of Dinh, Moore and Russell for Fourier sampling on code-equivalence coset states over (GL_k × S_n) ≀ Z_2 over F_2 needs q^(k·k) ≤ n^(n/5), which fails for self-dual and other high-rate binary codes. Exploit this opening: run strong Fourier sampling on single coset states over that group, where the large GL_k factor may carry usable signal, to obtain an exponential quantum speedup for self-dual code equivalence.
killer: The GL_k factor is removable: P ↦ RREF(G·P), the reduced row-echelon form of the column-permuted generator matrix, is computable in O(n^3) and is constant exactly on cosets of the code's automorphism group, so code equivalence becomes a hidden subgroup problem in the wreath product of S_n with Z_2 alone, the graph-isomorphism setting. There, for small automorphism groups, single-register strong Fourier sampling (Moore–Russell–Schulman) and entangled measurements on fewer than order n log n registers (Hallgren–Moore–Rötteler–Russell–Sen) give negligible information.
lesson: Before exploiting a failed hypothesis of a no-go theorem, check whether a canonical form removes the offending group factor; redundant ambient symmetry can create a spurious opening.
note: Record overclaims: the quoted bounds TV <= 1/(2 sqrt(n!)) and MI <= 1/(2 ln2 n!) are not standard results, '(S_n x S_n) wr Z_2' should read S_n wr Z_2 = (S_n x S_n) semidirect Z_2, and a large commutant dimension does not make quantum code equivalence 'strictly intractable'.

proposal: Attack graph isomorphism through the symmetric-group hidden subgroup problem: prepare coset states for the order-two subgroup generated by the isomorphism involution and recover it by weak Fourier sampling (measuring irrep labels), by strong Fourier sampling on one register in a well-chosen basis, or by a collective measurement on a few copies.
killer: Label probabilities depend only on characters, which are class functions, so weak Fourier sampling cannot tell conjugate subgroups apart, and all candidate involution subgroups here are conjugate. Moore, Russell and Schulman showed single-register strong Fourier sampling in any basis yields exponentially little information for such involutions, and Hallgren, Moore, Rötteler, Russell and Sen showed measurements on fewer than order n log n copies fail, leaving only highly entangled many-copy measurements with no known efficient implementation.
lesson: For hidden subgroup problems over S_n the barrier is computational, not informational: a viable route must supply an efficient entangled measurement on order n log n copies.
note: Record overclaims: commutant dimension is not a gate-count lower bound, #P-hardness of Kronecker coefficients does not imply hardness of a quantum measurement, and Hallgren et al. do not rule out measurements on order n log n copies.

proposal: For density-one modular subset sum with n random weights mod N ≈ 2^n, define a local target-indexed partner map: given a solution x for target t, output a solution x′ for a prescribed related target t′(t) that differs from x in at most εn coordinates, for a small constant ε. Conjecture that almost every solution has such a sparse partner, and use a coherent circuit for this map as a polynomial-time relation sampler inside Regev-style reductions from the dihedral coset problem.
killer: A Hamming ball of radius εn contains about 2^(H(ε)n) strings, each landing on a prescribed residue with probability about 1/N = 2^-n, so the expected number of sparse partners is 2^((H(ε)−1)n), exponentially small for every ε < 1/2. Sparse partners observed in small instances are finite-size coincidences.
lesson: Before building a local map between subset-sum solutions, compare the entropy of the neighborhood with the log of the modulus; below that threshold partners vanish asymptotically.

proposal: For a Boolean hidden-shift problem with g(x) = f(x ⊕ s), suppose the Fourier spectra of f and of its derivatives D_a f(x) = f(x) ⊕ f(x ⊕ a) are concentrated on polynomially many coefficients, so a Kushilevitz–Mansour or Goldreich–Levin learner finds the heavy coefficients from polynomially many samples. Treat this concentration, together with a heuristic sample budget, as a certificate that the quantum hidden-shift algorithm for f is efficiently dequantized.
killer: Learning the heavy coefficients of f identifies f, not s: the shift shows up only as phases (−1)^(s·y) on the coefficients of g, so one needs legal access to g and coefficients at frequencies y spanning F_2^n. If the heavy frequencies span a subspace V, then f is nearly invariant under shifts in the orthogonal complement of V and s is not identifiable from them; a real certificate needs a sampling reduction, an executed learner and a shift decoder.
lesson: Learning a function's spectrum is not learning its hidden shift; a dequantization claim must show identifiability and run a decoder on the actual shifted input.

proposal: Use pairs of index-ℓ quasi-cyclic binary codes (generator matrices built from ℓ circulant blocks) as hard instances of permutation code equivalence whenever the two codes agree on a fine permutation-invariant fingerprint, such as the multiset of weight profiles over coordinate tuples. Such fingerprint collisions between structured codes are natural benchmark rows for quantum coset-state attacks.
killer: Quasi-cyclic codes carry a polynomial-size group of structured equivalences (permuting the ℓ blocks, cyclic shifts within blocks, and multiplier maps), and fingerprint collisions in such families often arise because one code is the image of the other under these maps. Enumerating that group classically resolves such pairs, so they are structured controls rather than hard instances.
lesson: Before treating an invariant collision in a structured code family as hard, test equivalence under the family's own natural symmetry group and standard canonical forms.
note: Generalized from a single quasi-cyclic instance; the record's lesson states the general rule.

proposal: Code equivalence for codes with trivial automorphism groups is a hidden subgroup problem in the wreath product S_n ≀ Z_2 whose hidden subgroup has order two and encodes the hidden permutation. Because the irreducible representations and Fourier transform of this wreath product are explicit, measure single coset states in the Fourier basis (irrep label, then row and column) and decode the hidden permutation from the outcomes of independent single-copy measurements.
killer: All candidate hidden subgroups are conjugate, so irrep labels follow the same law under every hypothesis and carry no information. A single coset state is a uniform mixture with top eigenvalue |H|/|G|, so any one-copy measurement names the right permutation among n! with probability at most |H|/n! = 2/n!, twice blind guessing, and few-register bounds for this wreath product show the row and column outcomes are exponentially close to hypothesis-independent, so independent repetitions do not help.
lesson: For nonabelian hidden-permutation problems, compute the one-copy information bound first; it is usually negligible, so the real task is a growing-copy entangled measurement.

proposal: For density-one modular subset sum with n weights mod N ≈ 2^n, guess the carries produced in the lowest O(log n) bit positions (polynomially many choices) and encode the resulting exact low-bit constraints in a quotient lattice embedding. Conjecture that after this slicing the planted 0/1 witness is, for almost every instance, the unique shortest nonzero vector of the embedding, so an SVP solver or lattice reduction recovers it.
killer: Fixing O(log n) low bits removes only a poly(n) factor of competing lattice vectors. At density one the expected number of balanced ternary relations (vectors in {−1,0,1}^n with support about n/4 whose weighted sum vanishes mod N) no longer than the witness is 2^Ω(n), and a second-moment (Paley–Zygmund) argument shows such competitors occur on at least an inverse-polynomial fraction of instances, so isolation is not uniform.
lesson: To claim a planted vector is isolated, bound the expected number of short competing relations; slicing off logarithmically many bits removes only a polynomial factor from an exponential count.

proposal: Recover witnesses of density-one modular subset sum by nearest-plane (Babai) decoding with respect to an LLL-reduced basis of the kernel lattice, branching to the second-nearest plane at a constant number k of Gram–Schmidt levels. The resulting list has size n^O(k), and the conjecture is that it contains the planted 0/1 witness with inverse-polynomial probability over random instances.
killer: For a uniformly random 0/1 witness the Gram–Schmidt coordinates are uncorrelated with variance of order 1/‖b_i*‖^2, and after LLL reduction of a density-one kernel basis a constant fraction of the ‖b_i*‖ are O(1) (their geometric mean is about N^(1/n) ≈ 2), so the witness leaves the nearest plane at Θ(n) levels in expectation. A tail bound makes at most k deviations exponentially unlikely for constant k, so inverse-polynomial coverage needs depth Ω(n) and a list of size 2^Ω(n).
lesson: Before proposing bounded-depth enumeration, estimate on how many Gram–Schmidt levels a typical target deviates; if that number grows linearly, every fixed-depth list is exponentially unlikely to contain it.
note: Minor rigor gap in the record: Hoeffding is applied to deviation indicators that are only shown to be uncorrelated, not independent; the conclusion is plausible.

proposal: To measure the isotypic component of a state ρ under a group action U(g) projectively, run generalized phase estimation: prepare a reference register in the uniform superposition over G, apply U controlled on it, apply the quantum Fourier transform over G, and copy the resulting irrep label λ to an output register. Then discard the remaining reference registers (row and column indices), leaving the Lüders state P_λ ρ P_λ / Tr(P_λ ρ) for later measurements.
killer: Discarding the row and column registers amounts to measuring them: for fixed λ the Kraus operators act as matrix units on the irrep factor, so the instrument applies P_λ and then completely depolarizes (twirls) the irrep factor V_λ, keeping only the multiplicity part. The clean Lüders instrument requires copying λ and then running the whole phase-estimation circuit in reverse to uncompute the reference.
lesson: When a coherent subroutine is used to measure one label, uncompute its workspace rather than discarding it; discarded garbage turns a projective measurement into a twirl.

proposal: For the two-row irreducible representation (n−2, 2) of S_n, a multiplicity-two block in an inner (Kronecker) tensor product can be split by a parity operator with a proven spectral gap, giving an efficient circuit that resolves that block. Extend this parity-splitting construction into a general efficient quantum Kronecker transform that decomposes V_λ ⊗ V_μ into irreducibles of S_n with explicit multiplicity labels for arbitrary shapes λ and μ.
killer: A two-valued parity splitting resolves at most a two-dimensional multiplicity space, while Kronecker multiplicities for typical shapes are superpolynomial: Σ_ν g_λμν d_ν = d_λ d_μ with only e^O(√n) shapes ν forces some g_λμν ≥ sqrt(n!)·e^(-O(√n)). A general transform also needs bases for those multiplicity spaces, recoupling maps between bracketings, and a decoder, none of which the two-row case provides.
lesson: A construction certified for one low-multiplicity block is a test case, not evidence for a general transform; check how multiplicities grow on typical shapes first.

proposal: Each two-copy block of a collective coset-state measurement can be realized as a linear-combination-of-unitaries block encoding whose normalization is O(1) in expectation over natural inputs. Chain such blocks across the order n log n copies needed information-theoretically to obtain an efficient end-to-end collective measurement.
killer: LCU normalizations multiply under composition, so the success amplitude shrinks like the product of the per-block factors, and the per-pair factor concentrates near its typical value of about 4 (about 2 per copy), a constant above 1. Across Θ(n log n) blocks the total normalization is 2^Θ(n log n), which postselection or amplitude amplification must pay for.
lesson: Constant LCU normalization per block is affordable only at bounded depth; over a growing number of blocks it compounds exponentially unless a global construction avoids the product.

proposal: Benchmark quantum coset-state attacks on permutation code equivalence using pairs of random binary Goppa codes with matching parameters (for example extension degree 6, Goppa polynomial of degree 3, length 48), since Goppa codes underlie McEliece and resemble random codes under many generic invariants.
killer: Permutation equivalence is classically tractable for codes with small hull C ∩ C^⊥: Sendrier's support-splitting algorithm handles it efficiently, trivial-hull instances reduce to graph isomorphism, and random Goppa codes generically have small hulls. Polynomial invariants such as the dimension of the componentwise (Schur) square, hull data and dual weight-incidence signatures already separate inequivalent Goppa pairs.
lesson: Permutation code equivalence is hard only where support splitting fails, as for codes with large hulls; check hull dimension and Schur-square invariants before treating a code family as a hard source.
note: Generalized from a single Goppa instance to the family-level claim.

proposal: For the hidden subgroup problem in S_n with a hidden subgroup generated by a partial matching (an involution made of disjoint transpositions), the pretty good measurement on polynomially many coset states identifies the subgroup with high probability. Implementing that pretty good measurement then yields an efficient quantum algorithm for this coset-state problem.
killer: That success bound is information-theoretic, in the spirit of Ettinger–Høyer–Knill: it shows a good measurement exists, not that it can be implemented. The PGM is defined through the inverse square root of the average state over a superpolynomial hypothesis family acting jointly on many copies, it has no known compact description or circuit, and a polynomial-time entangled measurement plus a decoder would still have to be constructed.
lesson: Information-theoretic distinguishability from polynomially many copies is a starting point, not an algorithm; an efficient measurement, a compressed representation and a decoder must all be specified.

proposal: Standard lattice embeddings of modular subset sum (Lagarias–Odlyzko or Coster et al. style) followed by LLL, with tuned scaling constants and basis combinations, recover planted solutions of random density-one instances. Take this as a polynomial-time solver for an inverse-polynomial fraction of legal inputs, which is the average-case subset-sum assumption needed in Regev's quantum reduction from the dihedral coset problem.
killer: Embedding attacks provably work only below a critical density of about 0.94 even with an exact SVP oracle; at density one exponentially many short ternary relations compete with the witness, and LLL approximates SVP only within 2^O(n). Successes in small dimension reflect LLL acting like an exact SVP solver there and fade as n grows, and no uniform inverse-polynomial coverage bound is known.
lesson: Small-dimension lattice-reduction success says little near or above the critical density; a candidate solver must change the asymptotic short-vector geometry or come with a coverage proof.

proposal: To certify that the pretty good measurement separates hypotheses after the coset states have been compressed by a non-unitary channel (for instance by discarding or coarse-graining registers), it suffices to show that all cross-hypothesis overlaps Tr(ρ_a ρ_b) with a ≠ b are small.
killer: Pairwise PGM success bounds weigh each cross overlap against the state's own purity Tr(ρ_a^2), that is its inverse effective rank, and compression can make the states far from flat projectors. Overlaps alone mean nothing: two identical maximally mixed states of dimension D have overlap 1/D and cannot be told apart.
lesson: Normalize overlap-based distinguishability estimates by purity or effective rank, since small overlaps can come from spread-out states rather than distinguishable ones.
